name: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
tagline: DeepSeek rebuilds Flash as a 552B encoder-decoder with FP4 caching — MIT license, LICENSE file, no drama
description: The first V4.1-generation release: a 552B-backbone MoE that breaks with decoder-only orthodoxy in favor of a 40-layer causal encoder-decoder split (20+20), activating ~8B parameters while reading and ~16B while writing. Compressed Sparse Attention 2 plus an FP4 main KV cache brings memory down to roughly 890 bytes per token — about a quarter of DeepSeek-V4-Flash — behind a 1M-token input window with up to 384K tokens out, image-and-text input, and a continuously dialable reasoning-effort setting (1–100). Trained on 45T tokens; DeepSeek reports 90.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 74.2 on DeepSWE v1.1, and 90.9 on GPQA Diamond. A minor-update checkpoint, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, followed on October 17 under the same MIT terms.
why: The V4 line has now shipped three releases in a row with licensing done exactly the way we wish everyone did it: the HF weights repo carries a standalone LICENSE file — the standard, unmodified MIT text (1,084 bytes) — re-read directly this week, with the card tagged MIT and no acceptable-use rider or scale trigger anywhere. That makes the interesting part the architecture: a frontier lab betting that encoder-decoder plus four-bit caching is how you serve 1M-token agents cheaply, and publishing the weights and tech report the same day the API price drops to $0.15 per million input tokens off-peak. The October refresh repo carries the identical MIT file, so the whole V4.1 family stays clean.
useCases: Long-horizon terminal and coding agents — the 90.6 Terminal-Bench claim is exactly the workload the cache math targets
Million-token document and codebase analysis where FP4 KV caching makes self-hosted context windows affordable
Fine-tuning and distillation programs that want a current-generation MIT base with zero license negotiation
audience: Agent-infra teams, inference-optimization researchers, and anyone already serving the V4 line who wants the cache bill cut in four

setup.requirements: A serious multi-GPU download (the repo totals ~510 GB) even at 8–16B active; the new CSA2 + FP4 encoder-decoder path needs current framework builds — check your inference stack's V4.1 support before committing hardware. Hosted access via the deepseek-flash API if you'd rather not

license.notes: Re-verified 2026-11-01. The HF repo has a standalone LICENSE file of 1,084 bytes — raw text read directly: 'MIT License', 'Copyright (c) 2023 DeepSeek', standard permission grant, no riders — plus the mit tag and the card statement that repository and weights are MIT. There is no separate code repo: the inference/ and encoding/ folders live inside the same HF repo and are covered by the same file. No acceptable-use rider, scale trigger, or territory clause found. The refresh checkpoint deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (described on its card as a minor update, ~October 17) carries the same 1,084-byte MIT LICENSE and mit tag. No change to the license since the 2026-09-14 check. DeepSeek-V3 remains partial in our catalog under the old DeepSeek Model License; the V4/V4.1 line has now dropped those riders every release.

tally.stars: 4.8k HF likes and ~2.1M downloads last month on the main repo (the 1017 refresh adds ~4.3k likes and ~170k downloads); no GitHub repo — the code ships in the HF repo; community quantizations (GGUF, NVFP4) are widespread
tally.lastActivity: Released September 10, 2026; weights unchanged since, with the chat template, encoding, and inference folders patched through mid-October (HF repo last modified October 16); DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 followed October 17

limitations: Benchmarks are self-reported and the encoder-decoder + CSA2 + FP4 combination is genuinely novel — early framework support will be uneven and independent evals scarce; the card says 552B backbone while HF's safetensors metadata totals ~763B parameters (the difference is the non-backbone components), so read parameter counts carefully; 552B-class weights keep the download and the disk bill in deep water however few experts fire per token; and the 8B-read/16B-write asymmetry means throughput math from decoder-only models won't transfer directly.
take: Everyone else is optimizing decoder-only inference; DeepSeek just shipped an encoder-decoder frontier model with a four-bit cache and put MIT on the tin. If the architecture bet pays off, this is the shape of cheap million-token agents — and the license means you get to find out yourself.
